segments.text: Welcome to the Robotics Digest for October 31, 2026.
We cover 29 updates, including big moves in warehouse automation, autonomous factory building, and driverless truck scaling.
Tune in for the latest.
From Robotics & Automation News, Walmart expands Symbotic warehouse automation deal with $6 billion commitment.
This report details an expanded commercial agreement between Walmart and Symbotic, involving a commitment of approximately six billion dollars for further automation implementation.
The agreement will introduce advanced artificial intelligence enabled robotics capabilities across twenty-five United States regional distribution centers to facilitate global supply chain expansion.
Symbotic’s solutions, including BreakPack and SymMicro, utilize artificial intelligence to optimize the movement of inventory within these facilities.
Walmart intends to leverage this expanded automation to enhance e-commerce inventory management, increase storage capacity, and refine product flow.
This partnership is structured to improve customer service through increased speed and reliability throughout the supply chain operations.
This development signals continued integration of advanced robotics and artificial intelligence into large-scale logistics operations.
From Robotics & Automation News, Foundry Robotics raises one hundred million dollars in a Series A funding round to build America's first autonomous factory for assembly.
The company develops autonomous factories that integrate artificial intelligence powered robotic cells with established manufacturing expertise.
Foundry Robotics operates a manufacturing-as-a-service model that enables clients to transition rapidly from design to production without requiring extensive retooling.

The company concentrates its technological application on assembling complex electro-mechanical products for both the defense and commercial sectors, intending to stimulate U.S. manufacturing by offering flexible and scalable assembly capacity.
This development signals a focus on leveraging advanced robotics to redefine industrial production methodologies.
Future developments in autonomous manufacturing will be closely observed by industry analysts.
From Robotics & Automation News, Aurora outlines plan to scale to 30,000 driverless trucks.
This report details Aurora Innovation's objective to deploy over thirty thousand driverless trucks across the United States by the year 2030.
Aurora expects two hundred driverless trucks to be operational through Transport as a Service agreements by 2026, with additional deliveries planned for 2027.
Trucks utilizing Aurora's system have accumulated more than five hundred thousand driverless miles, and customers report an average of over two hundred twenty-five thousand miles annually.
The company is increasing hardware production, with Roush currently upfitting trucks at a rate of twenty per week.
The autonomous driving technology is presently integrated into International LT Series trucks and is under development for future incorporation into PACCAR trucks.
This development indicates ongoing progress in the commercialization and integration of autonomous driving systems within the commercial trucking sector.
From Humanoid.guide, AgiBot revenue nears 2 billion yuan as humanoid shipments rise.
This report details the financial performance and shipment statistics for the humanoid robotics sector during the first half of 2026.

AgiBot generated nearly two billion yuan in revenue over that period, corresponding to the shipment of nine thousand seven hundred humanoid robots, representing a forty-three point one percent share of global shipments.
The company indicated that these figures illustrate the capability to manufacture at scale and deploy robots effectively, stressing the importance of robust supply chains and ongoing maintenance.

Unitree Robotics also reported strong financial results, with revenue increasing substantially in the first nine months of 2026, a growth attributed to expanded manufacturing capacity, broader domestic and international applications, and the inclusion of long-term service solutions with hardware sales.
This data signals continued growth in the humanoid robotics market driven by increased manufacturing capability and service integration.
From Humanoids Daily, "Tesla Reportedly Plans Optimus Reservations for Early December".

This report details Tesla's reported plan to open reservations for the Optimus robot in early December, linked to the Humanoids Summit, with expectations that most units will initially be allocated to businesses.
Reservations are anticipated to occur before commercial deliveries, allowing the company to assess customer interest during the ongoing development phase.
Modar Alaoui indicated that the initial allocation of Optimus units is expected to favor commercial entities over individual consumers.
Specific details concerning reservation fees and consumer delivery terms have not been disclosed.
This move allows Tesla to gauge market demand prior to mass production rollout.
The industry should monitor subsequent announcements regarding delivery timelines and pricing structures.
From Humanoids Daily, "Tesla’s Optimus Data-Collection Effort Comes Into Focus After Scoble’s “Robot University” Claims".
This report examines claims made by Robert Scoble regarding Tesla's data collection efforts for the Optimus robot.
Tesla's internal job listings confirm the presence of motion-capture and data collection work across various facilities and shifts.
Scoble alleges that workers utilize suits equipped with up to forty cameras to gather this information, including recordings of domestic and automotive tasks.
Tesla's official postings establish the scope of the physical and operational work required of these personnel.
The actual utility of this collected data for robot learning remains distinct from the methods of its collection.
Developments in applied robotics data acquisition will continue to influence future machine learning approaches.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Humanoid expands collaboration with Nvidia to power its next generation of humanoid robots".

This report details a partnership between Humanoid and Nvidia to develop the computing foundation for forthcoming humanoid robots, focusing on a high-performance robotic edge runtime for onboard artificial intelligence processing.

The collaboration involves the integration of technologies such as the Nvidia Jetson Thor, Isaac OS, Holoscan Sensor Bridge, and associated Software Development Kits to facilitate the processing of sensor data and coordination of control.
This integration aims to streamline the system architecture and decrease latency for the real-world deployment of autonomous robots.
This partnership seeks to unlock new levels of autonomy for humanoid robotic systems.
The development signals a significant step in creating more capable and responsive autonomous robotic hardware.
From The Robot Report, "Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal".
This report details Agility Robotics' anticipated capital raise through a proposed special purpose acquisition company merger.
The company expects to raise four hundred sixty-five million dollars, incorporating funds from Churchill XI's trust account and a private investment in public equity led by Foxconn.
This anticipated funding is intended to support commercial expansion and address growing customer demand for the company's humanoid robots.

Agility plans to finalize the special purpose acquisition company transaction on November 4th, building upon existing efforts to achieve commercial deployments and securing multi-year orders for the Digit 5 humanoid.
This development indicates continued financial activity within the humanoid robotics sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, Maximo Robotics completes 300,000 tasks in utility-scale solar projects.
This report details the deployment of US-made, physical-AI robotics systems for construction tasks within utility-scale solar installations, achieving over three hundred thousand completed tasks.
Crew members operating with Max 4.0 systems demonstrated a rate of 2.5 times their manual installation rates per person per shift hour.
The company utilizes a performance-based robotics-as-a-service model where payment is based on completed tasks.

This deployment assists electricity companies in meeting energy demand within labor-constrained markets through the integration of AI models, robotics, and operational intelligence for task automation.
This development indicates a tangible application for autonomous systems in large-scale infrastructure development.
From Robotics & Automation News, AstraQua secured a one point three million dollar NASA contract for physical artificial intelligence development.

This contract is for advancing AstraSense technology designed for electric and hybrid-electric aircraft through the development of physical AI incorporating predictive health and operational self-awareness for autonomous systems.

The AstraSense technology enables machines to understand their own condition to make safer real-time decisions facilitating collaborative task management among robot teams, particularly in inspection scenarios.
This research emphasizes the implementation of low-power onboard intelligence and health-informed reasoning to facilitate autonomous operations.
This development indicates a focus on integrating self-monitoring into autonomous systems for enhanced safety and adaptability in future robotic applications.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Why Automated Cells Are Pulling Inspection Onto the Shop Floor".
This report details how automated cells are integrating inspection closer to the shop floor to improve efficiency.
Automated cells are bringing Coordinate Measuring Machines next to production to allow for rapid part checking.
This proximity shortens the feedback loop, enabling immediate adjustments to machining processes.
Shared data standards such as MTConnect allow robots and inspection equipment to communicate effectively.
This integration enables real-time quality control, catching variations early and increasing production confidence.
The implementation of this methodology demonstrates a significant shift toward proactive quality assurance in manufacturing environments.
This trend indicates a future where real-time data streams drive adaptive and highly precise automated production systems.
From Robotics & Automation News, Jungheinrich and Automha partner on warehouse automation.
This story details the formation of a strategic partnership to develop a two-way pallet shuttle designed for high-density storage.
The collaboration integrates Automha's shuttle expertise with Jungheinrich's system integration and software capabilities to create this novel solution.
This technology is engineered to serve as an economically viable entry point into warehouse automation by being designed to fit into existing facilities.

The shuttle technology facilitates increased storage density without requiring significant structural modifications, offering a method for customers to gradually modernize brownfield warehouses by integrating this shuttle technology with other automation systems.
This development signals a pathway for incremental automation within existing industrial infrastructure.
From Robotics & Automation News, Schaeffler and Wandelbots enter into technology partnership.

This partnership focuses on developing the Wandelbots NOVA open platform to apply artificial intelligence in industrial and humanoid robotics, with the projected result being a forty percent reduction in automation solution life cycle costs in manufacturing environments.

The collaboration involves the development of the NOVA platform, which serves as a unified system for implementing artificial intelligence across all Schaeffler plants globally, facilitating easier development, testing, and transfer of robotics applications.

This effort utilizes simulation technologies for application validation and establishes a skill store for systematic knowledge transfer, enabling the scalable use of physical AI and further digitalization across the global manufacturing network.
This joint endeavor signals a tangible path toward integrating physical artificial intelligence into widespread industrial automation.
From Robohub, Robot Talk Episode 168 – Advancing robotics with novel electronics, with Zlatka Stoeva.
This segment explores the development of flexible, stretchable, and soft printed electronics for dexterous robots through the work of DZP Technologies.
Zlatka Stoeva, specializing in materials chemistry, details how her company addresses the need for advanced materials and novel electronics in robotics.
The advancement originated from an ARIA-funded project specifically targeting printed electronics for dexterous robots.
The research focuses on integrating novel materials to create electronics capable of conforming to the complex shapes required by these machines.
This methodology involves the application of materials science to produce flexible substrates with integrated electronic components suitable for robotic applications.
The findings demonstrate a pathway for creating more adaptable and sophisticated robotic systems.
This research points toward the integration of advanced materials as a critical component in future autonomous machine development.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Pantheon Hand!".
This report details the specifications and reception of the Pantheon Hand, Stella Robot's flagship tendon-driven robotic hand, which achieved an overall score of seven out of ten.

The design incorporates a lightweight structure utilizing electric motors positioned outside the hand to reduce mass, resulting in a total weight of 0.29 kilograms and dimensions of two hundred thirty by one hundred ninety by fifty millimeters.
The hand features a five-finger configuration managed by single side pull cables that incorporate automatic tension adjustment.
Evaluation indicated a higher rating for Degrees of Freedom at four out of five than for Strength at three out of five, emphasizing dexterity and joint freedom over raw strength.
The product is currently in production with a listed price of three thousand five hundred US dollars.
This development signifies ongoing advancements in the practical application of lightweight, dexterous robotic manipulation systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Mantis Standart!".

This segment details the introduction of the Mantis Standart, a modular wheeled humanoid robot developed by Blue Worm in Xi'an, China, demonstrating a new entry point into wheeled humanoid development.
The robot measures one hundred forty centimeters in height and weighs fifty kilograms, designed for research, data collection, and light industrial tasks.
It incorporates two articulated arms, an adjustable waist, and supports up to twenty-two degrees of freedom, facilitating complex operations such as sorting and assembly.
The system is supported by ROS 2, MoveIt 2, and VR teleoperation, establishing an accessible framework for this type of robotics.
The platform is currently listed as in production with an initial cost of one thousand four hundred US dollars.
This development signals increased accessibility in wheeled humanoid robotics research and industrial application.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Lumen H1!".
This report details the introduction of the Lumen H1, a humanoid robot developed in China.
The robot stands at one hundred sixty-nine centimeters tall and weighs sixty-nine kilograms.
The Lumen H1 is equipped with over forty degrees of freedom and hands featuring five fingers, demonstrating capabilities in obstacle avoidance and sorting goods.
Safety systems incorporated into the design include LiDAR and RGB depth cameras, along with PLd level protection and a braking distance under one point seven meters.
The unit is offered in silver and yellow finishes and is targeted for service environments with a listed price of forty thousand United States dollars.
This development indicates ongoing advancements in practical, safety-conscious robotic manipulation for industrial applications.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Laborer C1!".
This report details the specifications and capabilities of the Laborer C1, a compact humanoid robot demonstrating advanced locomotion skills.
The Laborer C1 measures 138 centimeters and weighs 38 kilograms and is powered by electric joint actuators.
This robot has been assessed for abilities including obstacle avoidance, running up to one hundred meters, jumping, and landing maneuvers, as well as the capacity to sort goods.
The navigation performance was rated superior to manipulation capabilities, indicating a stronger focus on locomotion within human environments.
The unit is currently listed as being in production with a stated price of seventy thousand United States dollars, positioning it for public interaction.
This development suggests a growing focus on embodied movement skills in robotics research.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, TIAGo Pro!".
This segment reports on the introduction of the TIAGo Pro, a humanoid mobile manipulator from PAL Robotics designed for research and applications across various fields.
The robot possesses a humanlike upper body, two arms, a touchscreen face, and an omnidirectional wheeled base.
The device stands at 155 centimeters tall and weighs 80 kilograms, incorporating capabilities for obstacle avoidance, sorting, and product assembly.
It features torque sensing for compliant interaction and operates on an Ubuntu LTS operating system with ROS 2.
The TIAGo Pro incorporates a humanlike upper body structure, two arms, and a touchscreen face, supported by an omnidirectional wheeled base.
The robot is engineered to perform tasks including obstacle avoidance, sorting, and product assembly.
Advanced features include torque sensing for compliant interaction, and the system runs on an Ubuntu LTS operating system integrated with ROS 2.
This system demonstrates the integration of sophisticated hardware and software for complex manipulation tasks.
This development signifies progress in the field of mobile manipulation and embodied AI.
Further advancements in humanoid robotics and real-world application deployment are anticipated.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Lumen S1!".
This segment reports on the introduction of the Lumen S1, a compact humanoid robot developed in China demonstrating early capabilities in navigation and manipulation.
The Lumen S1 measures one hundred thirty centimeters and weighs thirty-five kilograms and features thirty-one body degrees of freedom powered by electric joints and five-fingered hands.
The robot incorporates NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX computing alongside sensing hardware including LiDAR to facilitate obstacle avoidance and the sorting of goods.
Preliminary performance ratings indicate the robot is in an early stage category with developing skills in navigation and manipulation tasks.
The unit is listed for production at a price of twenty thousand US dollars and is targeted toward educational and research markets.
This development signals ongoing progress in the integration of advanced sensing and actuation into practical humanoid robotics.
From Robotics & Automation News, Europe’s autonomous vehicle market gathers pace as robotaxi programs expand.
This report details the acceleration of autonomous vehicle development across Europe driven by expanding robotaxi, automated driving, and autonomous freight programs.
Companies including Bolt, Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen are advancing these technologies by utilizing Nvidia's computing platforms.
Bolt intends to commence real-world data gathering for robotaxis in Madrid in 2027 as part of a wider European deployment.
This activity encompasses both passenger vehicles and trucking, emphasizing the increase in levels of automation.
Safety validation processes, supported by frameworks such as Nvidia's Halos SAFE, are proving to be a critical element in this technological progression.
This development indicates a growing focus on integrated safety protocols within autonomous systems moving forward.
From Robotics & Automation News, Global Ocean Robotics Day highlights advances in autonomous underwater robots.

The event convened a symposium exploring the transformation of ocean research through artificial intelligence and autonomous robotics, featuring discussions on using vehicle trajectories for current mapping, autonomous docking simulations, and underwater robotic swarms.
Presentations further addressed bio-inspired robots, trustworthy multi-robot systems, and low-cost robotic fleets for ocean deployment.

Research presented at the symposium emphasized the capabilities of autonomous underwater robots in perception, navigation, and decision-making driven by onboard intelligence, fostering global collaboration in this field.
This development signals increased integration of artificial intelligence and robotics in deep-sea exploration methodologies.
From IEEE Spectrum - Robotics, "Video Friday: Spot Plays to Show Its Whole-Body Manipulation".

This feature showcases research demonstrating a contact-centric learning framework for versatile humanoid mobility in unstructured environments achieved through motion imitation and reinforcement learning.

Researchers presented a methodology focused on enabling robotic systems to navigate complex physical interactions by mimicking observed movements and optimizing actions through reinforcement learning principles.
This work explores novel approaches to achieving adaptable and effective whole-body manipulation in real-world settings.
Luxonis is simultaneously launching the OAK 4 FFC vision computer for developers building humanoid robots and drones.
Other featured projects included developments in robotic hands industrial navigation systems and bio-inspired amphibious robots highlighting progress across robotics and artificial intelligence.
This research indicates continued advancements in integrating physical interaction and machine learning for advanced robotic autonomy.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Open Telemetry - the next steps after logs with Matthew Macdonald-Wallace | Cloud Robotics WG Meeting 2026-11-16".
This segment reports on the proceedings of the Cloud Robotics Working Group meeting concerning the next steps following log management and the advocacy for Open Telemetry.
The meeting focused on achieving end-to-end visibility from the control platform to the end device through the adoption of Open Telemetry for metrics, logs, and traces.
During the discussion, the group finalized the Logging and Observability guide, which is pending final edits and community review before release.
Meeting details and recordings will be made available subsequently through the Cloud Robotics Hub.
This effort advances the industry's pursuit of comprehensive, traceable data streams in robotics systems.
From RoboPapers, "Ep#114: Oopsie Data"
reports on the development of a new resource for robotics research focusing on failure examples.
Claas Voelcker, Arpit Bahety, and Paul Zhou are presenting work concerning the collection of unsuccessful robot behaviors to address a data deficit in the field.
The research involves a systematic effort to collect these failures, such as unsuccessful manipulation trajectories, to create a large, community-driven open-source dataset.
This dataset aims to provide the necessary data for advancing complex areas of robotics research, particularly in the development of world models and reward model learning.
The methodology focuses on establishing a framework for systematically recording and sharing these failure instances across the robotics community.
This initiative seeks to make challenging data accessible for training more robust and capable artificial intelligence systems.
Future developments in robotics research will depend on the availability of such failure data for improved machine learning techniques.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Survey: where does your time go between laptop and robot? (3 min, results shared back)"
reports on a survey investigating the allocation of engineering time between laptop-based work and real robot implementation.

The survey aimed to determine where engineers spend their time when transferring software from simulation environments to physical robotic systems, focusing on integration, bring-up, timing, configuration, and debugging tasks across various frameworks.

The research involved surveying participants with twenty multiple-choice questions, collected anonymously, based on the system where the majority of time was spent, irrespective of the specific software framework utilized.
Aggregated results are scheduled for release approximately two weeks following the survey.
This data provides insight into the practical workflow challenges inherent in the transition from simulation to physical robotics engineering.
Future analysis of these results will inform development strategies for robotic software toolchains.
From The Robot Report, RoboBusiness 2026 recap details the event held in Santa Clara, California, which attracted over two thousand attendees interested in robotics developments.
The event, marking the twentieth anniversary and the final occurrence under the RoboBusiness brand, featured keynote panels, a Women in Robotics lunch, and an expo floor hosting industry discussions.
Sessions focused on the application of artificial intelligence in production robotics and the methods for operating autonomous robots at scale.
The Robot Operations Group also conducted RoboOpsCon26 the following day.
This gathering signifies continued focus on integrating advanced artificial intelligence into large-scale robotic systems.
Industry observers should anticipate further development in autonomous operational frameworks.
From Humanoids Daily, "What Is Worken? AGIBOT’s Proposed Measure of Productive Robot Work".
This segment details the proposal for Worken, a new measure designed to quantify productive robot operation through a specific formula.
The proposed measure combines the number of active robots, autonomous working hours, and an output efficiency ratio to calculate Effective Intelligent Work Hours.
The methodology distinguishes between independent task execution and nonproductive periods such as waiting or manual intervention within the operational cycle.
This calculation involves multiplying these three factors to arrive at the final metric.
The proposal explicitly notes that Worken is not a price for robot labor and necessitates the establishment of task-specific benchmarks for accurate measurement.
Practical application of this metric is contingent upon consistent operational data and subsequent testing to define reliable operational parameters.
The development of such metrics will influence how the AI and technology industry assesses robotic performance and efficiency moving forward.
From Robotics & Automation News, Bleu Robotics raises five million euros to scale humanoid robot deployment in factories.
The company secured this funding to scale its artificial intelligence models for industrial humanoid robots, with the goal of reducing the humanoid robot deployment process to one hour or less.
Bleu Robotics employs an abductive learning model which permits robots to learn novel tasks from only ten operator demonstrations, thereby bypassing the requirement for extensive training datasets.

This methodology facilitates cost-effective and scalable deployment by avoiding lengthy training cycles, allowing operators to teach robots new tasks directly using handheld devices within manufacturing environments.
This advancement points toward a shift in how complex tasks are taught to physical systems in industrial settings.
And that's all the circuits for today!
Hope your processing power was well-optimized.
Catch you in the next byte, and have a wonderfully algorithmic night!
